body.text: For several days, Phnom Penh has been living to the rhythm of the Francophonie. From the new Techo International Airport to the city center, Apsara dancers and Angkorian temples adorn banners celebrating both Cambodia and the French language. The slogans are exuberant: “Bienvenue au Royaume des Merveilles” (Welcome to the Kingdom of Wonders), “In French, please!” “The Khmer smile, the smile of the Francophonie.”

For Cambodia, hosting the 20th Francophonie summit on November 15-16 was a rare diplomatic showcase. Officials reported 81 confirmed delegations and 20 heads of state or government, including France’s Emmanuel Macron, Canada’s Mark Carney, Vietnam’s Tô Lâm, Rwanda’s Paul Kagame, and Félix Tshisekedi of the Democratic Republic of Congo. It was only the second Francophonie summit held in Asia, after Hanoi in 1997. Phnom Penh used the summit to highlight its historical role in the organization and broaden its diplomatic ties. Internal rivalries, however, drew attention away from the host’s ambitions.
Francophonie: A “Mini United Nations” With Cambodian Roots

The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) grew out of an ambition to turn a language inherited from empire into an instrument of cooperation among sovereign states. Cambodia’s Norodom Sihanouk was one of the project’s four founding figures, alongside Senegal’s Léopold Sédar Senghor, Tunisia’s Habib Bourguiba, and Niger’s Hamani Diori. The project began on March 20, 1970, with the creation of the Agency for Cultural and Technical Cooperation in Niamey, Niger, which became the OIF in 2005.

Today, the OIF brings together 90 states and governments: 53 full members, five associates, and 32 observers. Its membership also extends to subnational governments, including Quebec and other Canadian provinces, the U.S. state of Louisiana, and the French overseas territories of New Caledonia and French Polynesia. With biennial summits, a ministerial conference, a permanent council, and a secretariat headed by a secretary-general, the Francophonie resembles a “mini-U.N. General Assembly.” The Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie, the Agence universitaire de la Francophonie (AUF), television channel TV5MONDE, and Senghor University in Alexandria extend its wider institutional network.

The OIF’s 2026 report counted 396 million French speakers in the world and ranked French fourth globally, behind English, Mandarin, and Spanish. Nearly 65 percent live in Africa; speakers could approach 590 million by 2050. That demographic momentum broadens French’s appeal beyond its traditional strongholds.

The OIF’s remit spans language, cultural diversity, education, economic cooperation, democracy, and conflict prevention. The OIF connects partners across continents, even where few people speak French. In Cambodia, where French speakers account for less than 1 percent of the population, these ties help explain the summit’s diplomatic significance.
Behind the Celebrations, Political Divisions

But behind the festive welcome and the city’s cheerful atmosphere, deep political divisions are fragmenting the organization. The summit was due to choose the next secretary-general, usually selected by consensus. Among the four initial candidates, Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo was seeking a third term. But her candidacy faced opposition from the Democratic Republic of Congo amid the war in the Kivu region and Rwanda’s alleged support for M23 rebels. Kinshasa had threatened to withdraw from the OIF if she was reelected. The withdrawal of the country with the world’s second-largest French-speaking population – around 57 million people – would undermine the OIF’s credibility and significantly weaken its political standing.

The organization has already faced a series of departures. Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso chose to withdraw in 2025 after their participation was suspended following military coups. Their departures exposed tensions between the OIF’s democratic commitments, military rulers’ claims to sovereignty, and deteriorating relations with France.

Ultimately, rivalry in Africa’s Great Lakes region dominated attention in Phnom Penh. On November 16, the election of the OIF’s secretary-general was postponed for a year after members failed to reach a consensus. Rwanda’s Mushikiwabo will therefore remain in office until the rescheduled election, in which she will not stand. The postponement is unprecedented for an institution that had always selected its secretary-general by consensus. Although officials hailed the outcome as a compromise, the postponement exposed deep divisions that the agreement leaves unresolved.
Yet this Asian summit offered an opportunity to strengthen the Francophonie’s role in the Indo-Pacific, well beyond the contest over its leadership.
The Francophonie’s Indo-Pacific Reach

French is a minority language across most of the Indo-Pacific, but its institutional geography is extensive. In the southwestern Indian Ocean, it serves as a regional lingua franca connecting Réunion, Mayotte, Madagascar, Mauritius, Seychelles, and Comoros; Djibouti extends the network to the Horn of Africa. In the Pacific, French remains an official language in Vanuatu, New Caledonia, French Polynesia, and Wallis and Futuna.

Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam are full OIF members, reflecting their historical ties to France as former territories of French Indochina. Some members of their elites still speak fluent French, including Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihamoni.
Thailand and South Korea are observers. India’s Puducherry, where French retains an official role, joined the Parliamentary Assembly of the Francophonie.

For Asian members, French offers access to African markets, European and Canadian partners, and channels in which small and medium states can pursue their own priorities. The OIF’s regional relevance therefore rests on complementing existing security diplomacy with educational, scientific, and economic ties reaching beyond Southeast Asia. Such cooperation gives Asian participants a reason to engage between summits, regardless of their strategic outlook.
Giving Asia a Stake in the Future

The Francophonie’s future in Asia depends on the practical benefits it can offer. French has gradually lost ground in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia, whose elites increasingly favor English, the dominant international lingua franca and ASEAN’s working language. Francophone institutions have consequently sought to broaden their activities beyond language promotion.

Events held alongside the summit in Phnom Penh illustrated this shift. The free Francophonie Village in Wat Botum Park attracted an estimated 400,000 Cambodian visitors with performances, exhibitions, and national pavilions celebrating cultural diversity, while FrancoTech brought businesses and startups together around innovation. Ahead of the summit, universities and researchers gathered on November 10-12 for the Asia-Pacific Francophone Science Cycle (CSFAP), co-organized by Cambodia’s education ministry and the AUF.

The lasting value of these gatherings will depend on funded exchanges, recognized qualifications, and sustained research partnerships. Cooperation in public health, climate research, engineering, and multilingual AI could connect Asian expertise with needs across the francophone world, giving Asian partners a greater say in the OIF’s priorities through shared interests and tangible results.

Hosting the summit has given Cambodia diplomatic visibility. Whether it also marks a turning point for the Francophonie in Asia will depend on what its members build together once the delegations leave.
